498.title: Re'eh: open thy hand (Deuteronomy 15:7–8)
498.hook: don't harden your heart or shut your hand; "thou shalt surely open thy hand"
498.howItsDone: Some Jewish homes keep a tzedakah box, called a pushke, and drop coins in before the Sabbath; a tenth of income is a common measure, and Maimonides' eight levels are still taught.

segments.voice: Yesterday, re'eh: see the fork in the road, this day. Your line was see the choice. Today, a choice that comes up every time someone asks you for help.

A man is standing at the light with a cardboard sign. You see him from three cars back. And in the seconds before you reach him, a whole conversation can start up inside. Do I have cash? Will he spend it well? Is it safe to roll the window down? The light's about to change anyway. Sometimes, by the time the thinking is done, the moment's gone. The Torah knows that inner conversation, and it names the two body parts where it happens: the heart, and the hand.
screen: `A SIGN AT THE LIGHT.` → `THE CONVERSATION INSIDE.` → `THE HEART, AND THE HAND.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation: "thou shalt not harden thy heart, nor shut thy hand from thy needy brother; but thou shalt surely open thy hand unto him." Notice the order. The heart hardens first, then the hand closes. Giving starts inside, before any money moves. And notice the doubling. Surely open thy hand is, in Hebrew, patoach tiftach: open, you shall open. The rabbis read the double verb as open, and open again. Not once. The verse goes on: lend him sufficient for his need. His need, not your idea of his need. The word for all of this in Jewish life is today's word, tzedakah. It's often translated charity, but it shares a root with tzedek, justice, righteousness. Charity sounds like something extra you choose to do when you feel generous. Tzedakah is closer to what's right, what's owed, part of how a just society works. And how you give matters too. The path met Maimonides' eight levels of tzedakah earlier in the year; here's their shape again. Giving grudgingly is the lowest. Giving before you're asked is higher. Giving so neither side knows the other is higher still. And the highest of all: helping someone with a loan, a partnership or a job, so they won't need to ask again. A few verses later the Torah says plainly that there will always be poor people in the land. That's not a shrug. It's the reason the hand must keep opening.

segments.voice: Make two fists and feel them, tight and closed; then slowly open them, palms up, resting on your knees. Stay like that, and think of the last time someone asked you for help and you hesitated. Don't judge the conversation inside you; just notice it, palms open.
Tzedakah. Giving to those in need, from tzedek, justice. Not an extra, but part of what's right.

499.title: Re'eh: the release (Deuteronomy 15:1–2)
499.hook: every seventh year debts are released
499.howItsDone: In the land of Israel, observant Jewish farmers still keep the shmita year for the land, and many observant Jews sign a prozbul before the end of the seventh year so that loans aren't canceled.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tzedakah: the heart and the hand, open and open again. Your line was open thy hand. Today, a law that wipes the slate clean.

Picture the moment a student loan is finally paid off, or a medical bill forgiven. People describe it with their bodies. I could breathe again. A weight off my chest. Now imagine that moment built into the calendar. Every seven years, for everyone, at once. Not because a bank decided to be kind, but because the law said so. That's the seventh year in Deuteronomy. And the Mishnah remembers what happened when people actually tried to live by it.
screen: `PAID OFF: I COULD BREATHE.` → `BUILT INTO THE CALENDAR.` → `WHAT HAPPENED WHEN THEY TRIED.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation: "At the end of every seven years thou shalt make a release." The Hebrew word is shmita, a letting drop. Exodus already used that verb for the land: in the seventh year, let it drop, let it lie fallow. Deuteronomy uses it for debts. Each creditor lets go of what he lent to his neighbor, and doesn't press for it. Debt piles up. Without a reset, the poor get poorer and people get trapped. The release lets a whole society start over. But the Torah knows people. A few verses later it warns: don't let a base thought into your heart, saying the seventh year is close, and refuse to lend. If every loan will be wiped out in a year, why lend? By the time of Hillel, around the turn of the common era, that's what people were doing. The Mishnah says he saw that people had stopped lending to one another, and the poor were the ones getting hurt. So Hillel created a legal document called the prozbul. A lender could hand his debts over to the court, and debts held by a court weren't released. Lending started again. Some later teachers were uneasy, and the debate about Hillel's fix runs through the Talmud. But the motive is clear: a law meant to protect the poor had started to hurt them, and Hillel acted to protect them again.

segments.voice: Think of what someone owes you: maybe money, but more often an apology, a favor returned, a call back, credit for something you did. Let one of those debts come to mind, and notice the weight of holding it. Then ask what it would be like to let this one drop, not because they've earned it, but because the year has turned.
Re'eh. See. The portion that sets out the seventh-year release of debts, a whole society letting go at once.
Your line: release. Every seven years, a whole society got to start over. Day four hundred ninety-nine, done.

500.title: Re'eh: rejoice together (Deuteronomy 16:11, 14)
500.hook: rejoice at the festival with the servant, the stranger, the orphan and the widow
500.howItsDone: Jewish law treats joy on the festivals, especially Sukkot, as a commandment, and some families make a point of inviting guests, newcomers and people who would otherwise be alone to holiday meals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shmita, the seventh-year release, and Hillel's fix. Your line was release. Today is day five hundred, and fittingly, the Torah commands a party.

A really good wedding. The music, the dancing, the food. Now look at who's there. Family, old friends, coworkers. Who isn't? The neighbor who lives alone. The new guy at work who doesn't know anyone yet. Nobody left them out on purpose. They just weren't on the list. A celebration tends to draw its circle around the people already loved. The Torah's festival law draws that circle, then keeps going, naming people one by one until the guest list looks very different.
screen: `A REALLY GOOD WEDDING.` → `WHO WASN'T THERE?` → `THE CIRCLE KEEPS GOING.`

segments.voice: Deuteronomy sixteen walks through the three pilgrimage festivals: Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot. For Shavuot and Sukkot, it commands joy. In the old Jewish translation, of Sukkot: "And thou shalt rejoice in thy feast." The Hebrew word for that joy is today's word, simcha. Then the guest list. Thou, and thy son, and thy daughter, and thy servants, and the Levite, who, Deuteronomy says elsewhere, has no portion of land, and the stranger, and the fatherless, and the widow, who are within your gates. Rashi, the medieval commentator, counts them in two groups of four. Four are yours: son, daughter, manservant, maidservant. Four are God's: the Levite, the stranger, the orphan, the widow. And he imagines God saying: if you make Mine happy, I'll make yours happy. Maimonides, in a line from earlier this year, makes it sharper. In his law code he writes that someone who locks his courtyard gates and eats and drinks with his family, but doesn't feed the poor and the grieving, isn't having the joy of a commandment at all. He's having the joy of his stomach. So in Jewish law, simcha isn't only a feeling. It's something you make, and you can't fully make it alone, or only with your own. Joy, in this chapter, is measured partly by who else is at the table.

segments.voice: Five hundred days of this is worth a small celebration, and it's yours. Now picture the next gathering in your life, a birthday, a holiday meal, a Sabbath dinner, even coffee, and set Rashi's other four beside the table: the stranger, the one alone, the one grieving, the one without people nearby. Let one face come, and picture the seat beside you with them in it.
Simcha. Joy, the festival kind, commanded in Deuteronomy and made bigger by who you bring in.

501.title: Re'eh: as you were blessed (Deuteronomy 16:17)
501.hook: each gives according to the blessing they have received
501.howItsDone: The reading that ends with this verse is used on the last days of the pilgrimage festivals, and in many synagogues, when Yizkor is recited on those days, people pledge charity in memory of relatives who have died.

segments.voice: Yesterday, simcha: four of yours and four of God's at the festival table. Your line was rejoice together. Today, the last verse of Re'eh, about what each guest brings.

Someone at the office is leaving, and an envelope goes around for a gift. Somebody suggests everyone put in twenty dollars. And immediately it's awkward. For the manager, twenty is nothing. For the part-time assistant saving for rent, it's a real bite. A flat amount sounds fair, and isn't. A percentage sounds cold, and is fairer. Nobody quite knows how to say it out loud. The last verse of Re'eh says it, in a handful of words, about pilgrims arriving at the Temple three times a year.
screen: `THE ENVELOPE GOES AROUND.` → `TWENTY DOLLARS, FAIR OR NOT?` → `THE VERSE SAYS IT OUT LOUD.`

segments.voice: Three times a year, the chapter says, at Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot, every man of Israel is to appear at the place God chooses. And, in the old Jewish translation: "they shall not appear before the LORD empty." Every pilgrim brings something. But how much? The same sentence answers: "every man shall give as he is able, according to the blessing of the LORD thy God which He hath given thee." In Hebrew, ish k'matnat yado: each person according to the gift of his hand. No flat fee. The measure is what you've been given. The Mishnah, in tractate Chagigah, works it out for the festival offerings. Someone with many mouths to feed and little money brings what they can, shaped to their household. Someone with much brings more. Same command, different amounts. Notice the two sides. Nobody comes empty: even the poorest pilgrim brings something, and so stands in the courtyard as a giver, not just a receiver. And nobody hides behind a small number when they've been given a great deal. The verse shames no one. It asks one quiet question: what have you been blessed with? This verse also ends a Torah reading used on the last days of the festivals, and in many synagogues those are days when the memorial prayer, Yizkor, is said, and people pledge gifts in memory of those they've lost. Giving according to what you were given, including the people who gave it.

segments.voice: Take honest stock, and not just of money: time, health, a skill, free evenings, patience with kids. Which of these do you have more of this season than the people around you? 502.title: Shoftim: judges at the gates (Deuteronomy 16:18)
502.hook: judges in every town; Hasidic teachers read the gates as eyes, ears and mouth
502.howItsDone: Shoftim is usually read in synagogues around the start of Elul, the month before Rosh Hashanah, and Hasidic and other teachers often use its opening verse to speak about guarding the eyes, ears and mouth as part of the season's self-examination.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pilgrims who gave according to the gift of their hand. Your line was according to your blessing. Today a new portion, Shoftim, starts at the town gate.

Where would you go to settle a family dispute in the world of the Bible? Not a building with columns. The gate. In the Bible, a town gate is more than a door in the wall. Elders sit there. Deals are witnessed there. In the book of Ruth, Boaz goes up to the gate, sits down, and settles a family matter in front of ten elders. Everything that comes into the town, people, goods, news, trouble, comes through the gate, and whoever sits there decides what to do about it. That's where the new portion begins.
screen: `TO SETTLE IT, GO TO THE GATE.` → `BOAZ SITS AT THE GATE.` → `EVERYTHING COMES THROUGH.`

segments.voice: The first verse, in the old Jewish translation: "Judges and officers shalt thou make thee in all thy gates." Shoftim means judges, and it names the portion. The plain sense is civic. Every town needs courts, and people to enforce what courts decide, right where life passes through. Justice shouldn't be a long trip to a distant capital. It should sit at your own gate. But notice the odd little word thee. In Hebrew, lecha: for yourself. Judges for yourself? Hasidic masters, building on earlier mystics, read the verse inward. A person is a town too, they said, with gates of their own: the eyes, the ears, the mouth, and some add the nostrils. Everything that enters you comes through those gates, what you look at, what you listen to, what you take in. And what leaves you goes out through one of them: what you say. So set judges at your gates. Not to shut them; a town with its gates welded shut starves. But to notice what's coming in and going out, and to decide. And the calendar helps. Shoftim is usually read around the start of Elul, the month before Rosh Hashanah, a season set aside for taking stock. A portion about courts at the gates arrives just as people start judging their own year.

503.title: Shoftim: justice, justice (Deuteronomy 16:20)
503.hook: "Justice, justice shalt thou follow"; the doubled word means just ends by just means
503.howItsDone: Tzedek tzedek tirdof is often quoted in Jewish life, inscribed in some synagogues and courthouses and cited by Jewish organizations working for social and legal justice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, judges at the gates: the town's and your own. Your line was guard your gates. Today, two verses later, a line that says one word twice.

It turns up on posters, on courthouse walls, on protest signs. Two words, repeated: justice, justice. In a language where one word is usually enough, the Torah says this one twice, and close readers have asked why. The Talmud asks. Centuries later, the Hasidic teachers ask again. The answers don't cancel each other out. They stack, like layers, each one turning the doubled word a little and catching a different light.
screen: `ON A POSTER, A WALL, A SIGN.` → `ONE WORD, SAID TWICE.` → `THE ANSWERS STACK.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation: "Justice, justice shalt thou follow, that thou mayest live, and inherit the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee." In Hebrew, tzedek tzedek tirdof. Tzedek is today's word: justice, rightness. It's the root of tzedakah, from a few days ago. And tirdof doesn't really mean follow. It means pursue, chase, run after. Justice isn't something you wait for. Now the double. The Talmud, in Sanhedrin, offers a few readings. One: the first justice is strict law, the second is compromise. A court should know when to rule, and when to help two sides settle. Another: pursue a good court; travel to the wisest judges. And a reading that became famous much later, often attributed to the Hasidic teacher Rabbi Simcha Bunim of Peshischa: pursue justice justly. Just ends by just means. You can't chase justice by cheating, by lying, by trampling people on the way. The road has to be as just as the place you're trying to reach. The verse right before gives a sharp example: a judge must not take a gift, because a gift blinds the eyes of the wise. A bribe doesn't just tempt; it changes what you can see. So the doubled word guards both ends. The goal must be just, and so must the road.
screen: `TZEDEK TZEDEK TIRDOF.` · `NOT FOLLOW: PURSUE.` · `STRICT LAW, AND COMPROMISE.` · `JUST ENDS BY JUST MEANS.` · then, large: `JUSTICE, JUSTICE.`

segments.voice: Think of something you're in the right about, a dispute with a sibling, a cause you care about, an argument at work, and look only at the means. Have you pursued it with accurate words or exaggerations, with respect for the other side or contempt, with patience or pressure? Find the one place where the road has been less just than the goal.
Tzedek. Justice, rightness. Said twice in Shoftim, and pursued, not waited for.
Your line: justice, justice. The goal and the road there both have to count. See you tomorrow.

504.title: Shoftim: even the king reads (Deuteronomy 17:18–20)
504.hook: the king writes his own copy of the Torah so his heart isn't lifted up
504.tomorrow: Shoftim: is the tree a man? (Deuteronomy 20:19)
504.howItsDone: Jewish law counts writing a Torah scroll as a commandment for every Jew; many fulfill it today by sponsoring or writing a single letter in a community's new scroll, and the king's special scroll is discussed in the Talmud and Maimonides.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tzedek tzedek tirdof: pursue justice, and pursue it justly. Your line was justice, justice. Today, the law for the most powerful person in the land.

In the ancient world, a king was the law. His word settled things. His image was on the coins. Scribes carved his victories into stone. The idea that a king might have to sit down with a pen and copy out somebody else's law, by hand, every word, and then read it every day of his life, would have sounded absurd in most royal courts. Deuteronomy's chapter on kings is short, and mostly a list of limits. And it ends with an assignment.
screen: `THE KING WAS THE LAW.` → `COPY SOMEONE ELSE'S LAW?` → `A CHAPTER OF LIMITS.`

segments.voice: First the limits. If Israel sets a king over itself, he must not pile up horses, or take many wives, or heap up silver and gold. Power, pleasure, money: the three things kings usually collect. Then the assignment. In the old Jewish translation: when he sits on his throne, "he shall write him a copy of this law in a book." And it shall be with him, "and he shall read therein all the days of his life." Why? The verse says it plainly: "that his heart be not lifted up above his brethren." The king is still one of them. The Talmud, in Sanhedrin, adds that the king writes a scroll of his own, kept with him wherever he goes, even into battle. And it notes that every Jew is commanded to write a Torah scroll; the king just has an extra one. The phrase for a copy of this law is mishneh hatorah. It's where Deuteronomy gets its Greek name, second law. Over a thousand years later, Maimonides borrowed the same words for his great law code, the Mishneh Torah. The king reading every day is a picture of power under something bigger than itself: not the king's word over the law, but the law over the king's word. Reading isn't a reward for the powerful. It's a brake.
screen: `NOT HORSES, WIVES, OR GOLD.` · `WRITE HIM A COPY OF THIS LAW.` · `NOT LIFTED ABOVE HIS BROTHERS.` · `MISHNEH TORAH: SECOND LAW.` · then, large: `EVEN THE KING READS.`

segments.voice: Think of a place where you hold some power: a parent, a manager, the one who knows most in the room, the oldest sibling. Bring to mind a line, from scripture, a teacher or your grandmother, that puts that power back in its place, something like: you are one of them. Say it slowly, twice, and let it sit above you for a minute.
Shoftim. Judges. The portion where even the king must write the law down and read it every day.
Your line: even the king reads. A week of tzedakah, the release, simcha, giving by your blessing, judges at the gates, and justice twice. That's day five hundred four.
